newsitem.title: UK: Major in pre-poll pitch for UK have-nots' votes.
newsitem.headline: Major in pre-poll pitch for UK have-nots' votes.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Saturday rallied his Conservative Party for battle at an imminent election with a plan for a welfare revolution which would enable the have-nots to share Britain's economic success.

In a speech to the last big Conservative gathering before Britons cast their votes, Major set out his vision of a people's Britain where "everyone can make their own choices and live their own lives."

And he insisted despite opinion polls putting the Labour opposition more than 20 points ahead, that his party would win a fifth consecutive term of office in "one of the most crucial general elections we have known for generations".

"We'll win because our policies work and Labour's don't, because we say what we believe in and Labour don't, because we're proud of our record and they're trying to hide their past," Major told the meeting of Conservative Central Council.

Major is widely expected to call an election for May 1. The Conservatives will then face their toughest fight since Margaret Thatcher came to power in 1979, against a resurgent Labour party under moderate leader Tony Blair.
They will be battling against a feeling in the country that the economic revolution which began under Thatcher has benefited the fortunate few, but done little to improve the lot of ordinary Britons.
Major strove to dispel the idea that after 18 years in office, his party had run out of steam, and that it was therefore time for Labour to show what it can do.

"Britain has changed -- from being a European basket case to an international role model...so when you hear siren voices wailing It's time for a change', fix them in the eyes and challenge this nonsense," he said.
Major said the Conservatives planned radical changes adding up to the greatest "move forward in public welfare" since a Labour government brought in a welfare state in the late 1940s.
"I dream of a people's Britain in which all the people --not only the confident and well to do -- can make their own choices and mould their own lives," he said.

"The Conservatism I'm talking about isn't just for the lucky, the fortunate, the able, the self-confident. It's for everyone -- for those for whom life is a struggle, for those who don't have the best education, don't have a decent home, don't live in a safe neighbourhood, don't have a job."

In the past two weeks, the Conservatives have set out plans for private pensions which they say will give people a more prosperous old age, and for making the private sector largely responsible for delivering social services to the elderly.

"I believe it is time for (a) great move forward in public welfare, to bolster social security with personal and family security, to build alongside state provision growing private wealth," Major said.
Major, who received a rapturous standing ovation from the constituency officials attending the meeting, made no mention of confidence-sapping comments by two of his MPs on Friday.

John Biffen and Edwina Currie both speculated openly about what would happen following a Conservative election defeat, with Biffen saying the scale of the party's losses could be enough to remove some leading cabinet ministers from parliament.
But Major said a Labour win would dash the hopes of Britons.
"If Mr Blair ever walked in through the most famous door in the world (10 Downing Street), half the hopes of Britain would disappear out the back," he said.
He said "18 years of sound government and sheer hard work by the British people" had transformed the economy.
"We must not throw it away, throw it away with the wrong economic policy," he said.
